Hi, Dr. ____. Thank you for seeing me. Um, well, I guess what brings me in is... I just feel like I can’t settle in my own body anymore. It's hard to explain, but it’s like this physical impossibility for me lately. I mean, I’m at home most of the day right now, and you’d think I’d have all the time in the world to just get things done, but whenever I’m supposed to sit quietly and handle, you know, paperwork or our shared household plans—like the budgeting, or organizing the family calendar, things I really should be able to just sit and do—I just can't. 

I'll sit down at the kitchen table with the laptop or the bills and it's like my skin is buzzing. I shift around, I get up to get water, I remember a load of laundry, and I just cannot physically force my body to stay in the chair and be still. It’s incredibly frustrating because I have a bachelor's degree, I know how to read a spreadsheet, I know how to manage a project, but my body just completely rebels if I try to sit quietly and focus on it. It's just this constant, restless feeling, and it's really starting to take a toll on my marriage and just my general sanity, honestly, because I just want to be able to sit down and finish a simple task.

Um, act on impulses? No, I don't... I don't really think I do that, actually. I mean, when I hear "acting on impulse," I tend to think of people who, I don't know, suddenly book a trip to Vegas or buy a boat without telling their spouse, or just blurt things out that ruin a dinner party. I never just jump into things blindly. So, no, I wouldn't say I act without thinking first. It's really more that my body is just constantly restless while my brain is doing all that thinking, if that makes sense? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Oh, interrupting... well, that’s... that’s actually a really sore subject in our house right now, to be completely honest. I mean, I care so much about being respectful. I really, really do. I was raised to be polite, and I know how rude it is to cut people off. I hate when people do it to me. But, despite knowing all of that, and despite genuinely trying to be a good listener... yes. Yes, I do it all the time, and it drives my husband absolutely up the wall. 

It’s like... okay, so picture this. My husband will be telling a story, right? Maybe he’s talking about something that happened at work, or he’s on the phone with his sister, and he’ll pause for just a half-second to take a breath or find a word. And my brain just... fills in the blank. And before I even have the conscious thought of, "Oh, I should wait my turn," the words are already out of my mouth. I’ll just jump right into his conversation, or I’ll finish his sentence for him, or I’ll completely derail his point because a thought popped into my head and it just *had* to come out right that exact second. 

It’s not like I’m sitting there thinking, "What I have to say is more important than what he’s saying." It’s not malicious at all. It’s just... the response just bursts out of me before I’ve managed to put the brakes on and make myself wait. It’s like there’s no filter between the thought forming in my brain and my mouth opening to say it. 

Just the other day, we had some neighbors over for coffee—just a casual thing on the patio—and the husband was explaining this whole complicated issue they were having with their landscaping contractor. And in the moment, I’d realize what I did, and I’d feel terrible, and I’d apologize and say, "I’m so sorry, please go on," but then three minutes later, I’d do it again! It’s just so incredibly frustrating because I know better, but it’s like my mouth is moving faster than my self-control.

Oh, definitely. It is actually something that comes up a lot. My husband, especially, is always pointing it out. Because, well, take church meetings for example, or even just nice, sit-down family dinners. Especially if it is extended family and you are supposed to be, you know, on your best behavior. I try so incredibly hard to just sit there and look composed. I really, really do. I will literally tell myself in my head to just sit still, fold my hands, and be normal. 

But it is like this physical impossibility for me. If you actually watch me during one of these things, I am constantly, and I mean constantly, twisting my wedding ring around and around my finger. Or I will be bouncing my foot under the table, which sometimes shakes the whole floor and makes the silverware rattle, or I am just endlessly shifting my weight around in the chair. I will cross my legs, then uncross them, then tuck one leg under me, then sit forward, then lean back. 

And people absolutely notice it. My mother-in-law will ask if I am uncomfortable, or if the chair is too hard, and I always have to make up some excuse about my back aching or needing to stretch because I do not want to admit that I just literally cannot sit normally like everyone else. It is exhausting, honestly, because in my head I am trying so hard to project this image of a calm, collected adult woman, but my body is just rebelling the entire time. And it is not just the big movements, it is the little ones too, the ring twisting, the foot tapping. I just do not understand how other people can just sit there like statues. They just sit and listen, and I am practically doing a whole workout in my seat just trying to keep all that nervous energy contained. So yes, people definitely describe me that way, because it is pretty impossible to hide no matter how hard I try to look put together.

Oh, absolutely. That is... yes, that is a huge thing for me. A really, really big struggle, honestly. It’s so frustrating because I genuinely want to be productive and stay on top of things, but my brain just does not want to cooperate. 

Like, I love to read. I really do. I have this book club I joined with some of the other moms from my kids' school—we meet once a month on Tuesdays, usually at someone's house—and I always have the best intentions of actually finishing the book. I'll make myself a cup of tea, I'll sit down in my favorite chair by the window where the lighting is good, and I'll open up to a new chapter. And for the first couple of minutes, I start out completely fine! I’m following the plot, I’m interested in the characters. But then... it's like I don't even realize it's happening at first. Just a few minutes later, I’ll suddenly realize that I’m just staring at the exact same paragraph over and over again, and absolutely none of it went in. My eyes were moving across the page, I was physically looking at the words, but my brain just completely stopped recording the information. I’ll have to flip back two or three pages just to figure out where I actually checked out. 

And it’s not just with fun things like reading for a book club. It happens with the important, day-to-day stuff, too. Since I’m not working right now, I handle a lot of the household organizing and the school committee stuff. So, I'll get these long planning emails from, say, the PTA president. She's lovely, but she writes these massive, detailed updates about the spring carnival or the logistics for the teacher appreciation luncheon. I’ll sit down at my laptop to read it, completely determined to get it done, and I start out fine. But halfway down the screen, the exact same thing happens. I’m just staring at a block of text about volunteer shifts or napkin colors, and nothing is registering. 

It takes me forever to get through anything that requires me to just sit and focus, because I have to keep rereading the same sentences four or five times before the meaning actually sticks in my head long enough for me to process it. It’s not that I don’t care about the spring carnival, you know? It’s just like my attention span has this tiny little expiration timer on it, and once those first few minutes are up, the timer goes off and my focus just completely dissolves, even if I'm staring right at the thing I'm supposed to be concentrating on. So, yes, to answer your question, sustaining attention is definitely a major, major issue for me.

They’d say I was bright, but they’d write these notes saying I talked out of turn constantly, or that I just seemed completely unable to stay seated during the lessons. Like, reading time was a nightmare for me. I’d be up on my knees, or fidgeting with my shoelaces, or turning around to talk to whoever was behind me. I just couldn't stay in my little assigned square on the rug. So, yeah, it’s really this exact same physical feeling I have now of just not being able to stay glued to the chair, just playing out in a forty-one-year-old's life instead of a third grader's.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulses without thinking first?\n\nPatient: Um, act on impulses? No, I don't... I don't really think I do that, actually. I mean, when I hear \"acting on impulse,\" I tend to think of people who, I don't know, suddenly book a trip to Vegas or buy a boat without telling their spouse, or just blurt things out that ruin a dinner party. And that’s really not me at all. \n\nEven though I have all this nervous energy and I’m constantly buzzing around the house like I mentioned, I’m actually pretty careful about the decisions I make and the things I actually *do*. Like, with the family budget I was talking about earlier—I might not be able to physically sit in the chair long enough to finish the spreadsheet in one go, but I’m certainly not going out and blowing our savings on a whim just because I felt like it. I actually think things through a lot. Probably too much, if you ask my husband! \n\nSometimes I think he actually wishes I *would* be a little more spontaneous, because I tend to over-analyze everything. Like, if we're deciding on a summer camp for the kids, I'll have ten different tabs open on my laptop researching every single detail, reading all the reviews, checking the counselor-to-kid ratios, before I ever make a move to register them. I never just jump into things blindly. So, no, I wouldn't say I act without thinking first. It's really more that my body is just constantly restless while my brain is doing all that thinking, if that makes sense? But yeah, as far as just doing things on impulse, I really haven't noticed that being an issue for me.\n\nDoctor: Do you often interrupt other people when they’re talking?\n\nPatient: Oh, interrupting... well, that’s... that’s actually a really sore subject in our house right now, to be completely honest. I mean, I care so much about being respectful. I really, really do. I was raised to be polite, and I know how rude it is to cut people off. I hate when people do it to me. But, despite knowing all of that, and despite genuinely trying to be a good listener... yes. Yes, I do it all the time, and it drives my husband absolutely up the wall. \n\nIt’s like... okay, so picture this. My husband will be telling a story, right? Maybe he’s talking about something that happened at work, or he’s on the phone with his sister, and he’ll pause for just a half-second to take a breath or find a word. And my brain just... fills in the blank. And before I even have the conscious thought of, \"Oh, I should wait my turn,\" the words are already out of my mouth. I’ll just jump right into his conversation, or I’ll finish his sentence for him, or I’ll completely derail his point because a thought popped into my head and it just *had* to come out right that exact second. \n\nIt’s not like I’m sitting there thinking, \"What I have to say is more important than what he’s saying.\" It’s not malicious at all. It’s just... the response just bursts out of me before I’ve managed to put the brakes on and make myself wait. It’s like there’s no filter between the thought forming in my brain and my mouth opening to say it. \n\nJust the other day, we had some neighbors over for coffee—just a casual thing on the patio—and the husband was explaining this whole complicated issue they were having with their landscaping contractor. I’d be like, \"Oh, did you try calling this other guy?\" or \"Wait, didn't they say they were going to use the blue stone instead of the pavers?\" And every time I did it, I could see my husband giving me that *look* out of the corner of his eye. Oh, yes, absolutely. That internal feeling... that's exactly it. It's actually a big part of what finally made me decide to come in and talk to someone, because I just feel like I can't settle in my own body anymore. It's this constant, buzzing sort of tension right under my skin. 

It's the worst when I'm supposed to be sitting quietly and handling things, you know? But me? I sit down next to him, and almost immediately, I feel this... this pressure building up inside my chest and my legs. It's not always that I'm actually getting up and running around the room, though sometimes I do suddenly remember that I need to go check the laundry or grab a glass of water just to have an excuse to stand up. But even when I force myself to stay planted in the chair next to him, internally, I feel like a motor that's just revving and revving with nowhere to go. My mind is screaming at me to move, to stretch, to just *do* something other than sit there looking at the calendar. 

I'll try to take deep breaths, or I'll grip the edge of the table, just trying to force that restless feeling down so we can finish figuring out who is picking up our youngest from soccer practice on Thursday. But it's so uncomfortable. It's physically uncomfortable to just exist in my own skin during those moments. It's like my body is telling me that sitting still is somehow an emergency that I need to escape from. So yes, even when I'm physically staying in one spot, inside, I'm just pacing back and forth, completely unable to just settle down and be at peace.

So yes, people definitely describe me that way, because it is pretty impossible to hide no matter how hard I try to look put together.\n\nDoctor: Do you also have trouble sustaining attention and concentrating on tasks?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. That is... yes, that is a huge thing for me. A really, really big struggle, honestly. It’s so frustrating because I genuinely want to be productive and stay on top of things, but my brain just does not want to cooperate. \n\nLike, I love to read. I really do. I have this book club I joined with some of the other moms from my kids' school—we meet once a month on Tuesdays, usually at someone's house—and I always have the best intentions of actually finishing the book. I'll make myself a cup of tea, I'll sit down in my favorite chair by the window where the lighting is good, and I'll open up to a new chapter. And for the first couple of minutes, I start out completely fine! I’m following the plot, I’m interested in the characters. But then... it's like I don't even realize it's happening at first. Just a few minutes later, I’ll suddenly realize that I’m just staring at the exact same paragraph over and over again, and absolutely none of it went in. My eyes were moving across the page, I was physically looking at the words, but my brain just completely stopped recording the information. I’ll have to flip back two or three pages just to figure out where I actually checked out. \n\nAnd it’s not just with fun things like reading for a book club. It happens with the important, day-to-day stuff, too. Since I’m not working right now, I handle a lot of the household organizing and the school committee stuff. She's lovely, but she writes these massive, detailed updates about the spring carnival or the logistics for the teacher appreciation luncheon. I’ll sit down at my laptop to read it, completely determined to get it done, and I start out fine. But halfway down the screen, the exact same thing happens. I’m just staring at a block of text about volunteer shifts or napkin colors, and nothing is registering. \n\nIt takes me forever to get through anything that requires me to just sit and focus, because I have to keep rereading the same sentences four or five times before the meaning actually sticks in my head long enough for me to process it. It’s not that I don’t care about the spring carnival, you know? It’s just like my attention span has this tiny little expiration timer on it, and once those first few minutes are up, the timer goes off and my focus just completely dissolves, even if I'm staring right at the thing I'm supposed to be concentrating on. So, yes, to answer your question, sustaining attention is definitely a major, major issue for me.\n\nDoctor: Before age 12, did you have these same kinds of attention or activity problems in more than one place, like both at home and at school?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Mine was just a complete disaster zone of crumpled up worksheets and stray crayons and old snack wrappers. \n\nAnd oh my goodness, the forgotten permission slips. My mother used to get so incredibly frustrated with me because I would pull out a permission slip for a field trip or a pizza day that was shoved all the way at the very bottom of my backpack, completely destroyed and unreadable, and it would already be three days past the deadline. It was the exact same story at home, which used to drive my dad crazy. My parents were always getting onto me for jumping up from the dinner table before we were excused, or I would be sent upstairs to clean my room and my mom would come in an hour later and I would be playing with some old toy I found under the bed, with the room just as messy as when I started. So yes, it was definitely happening in both places. It is like I have just always been this way, even when I was seven or eight years old, just constantly buzzing around and losing track of absolutely everything I was supposed to be doing.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel internally restless or like you need to move around, even when you’re trying to sit still?\n\nPatient: Oh, yes, absolutely. That internal feeling... that's exactly it. It's actually a big part of what finally made me decide to come in and talk to someone, because I just feel like I can't settle in my own body anymore. It's this constant, buzzing sort of tension right under my skin. \n\nIt's the worst when I'm supposed to be sitting quietly and handling things, you know? Oh, completely. I mean, like I was saying before about jumping up from the dinner table when I was seven or eight, it was definitely there back then. I was always in motion. But it’s funny, because as you get older, you realize you can't exactly just go wandering off during a sermon or a nice dinner whenever you feel like it. She was always having to call the school office to beg them to let me go on the trip anyway.\n\nAnd the parent-teacher conferences were always exactly the same, year after year. My parents were constantly getting notes sent home from my teachers saying that I talked out of turn, or that I seemed completely unable to stay seated during lessons. The teachers would always tell my parents that I was a sweet girl, but I was just constantly interrupting the lesson or wandering around the classroom to sharpen my pencil for the fifth time or go look out the window. \n\nAnd it definitely was not just at school, either. It was the exact same story at home, which used to drive my dad crazy. My parents were always getting onto me for jumping up from the dinner table before we were excused, or I would be sent upstairs to clean my room and my mom would come in an hour later and I would be playing with some old toy I found under the bed, with the room just as messy as when I started. So yes, it was definitely happening in both places. That internal feeling... that's exactly it. It's actually a big part of what finally made me decide to come in and talk to someone, because I just feel like I can't settle in my own body anymore. It's this constant, buzzing sort of tension right under my skin. \n\nIt's the worst when I'm supposed to be sitting quietly and handling things, you know? Like, my husband and I try to sit down on Sunday evenings to go over the shared household plans for the week—the kids' schedules, the meal planning, the budget, all that necessary paperwork that keeps a family running. I sit down next to him, and almost immediately, I feel this... this pressure building up inside my chest and my legs. But even when I force myself to stay planted in the chair next to him, internally, I feel like a motor that's just revving and revving with nowhere to go. My mind is screaming at me to move, to stretch, to just *do* something other than sit there looking at the calendar. \n\nI'll try to take deep breaths, or I'll grip the edge of the table, just trying to force that restless feeling down so we can finish figuring out who is picking up our youngest from soccer practice on Thursday. But it's so uncomfortable. It's physically uncomfortable to just exist in my own skin during those moments. It's like my body is telling me that sitting still is somehow an emergency that I need to escape from. So yes, even when I'm physically staying in one spot, inside, I'm just pacing back and forth, completely unable to just settle down and be at peace.\n\nDoctor: Were you also this fidgety and unable to sit still as a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, completely. I mean, like I was saying before about jumping up from the dinner table when I was seven or eight, it was definitely there back then. I was always in motion. Society kind of expects you to sit down and act like an adult. So that childhood need to run around just sort of... morphed into this constant, endless fidgeting. \n\nIt’s like that internal energy I mentioned still has to go somewhere, you know? I really put a lot of effort into trying to look like a normal person who can just sit peacefully through a service or a long meal. \n\nBut if you actually watch me during those times, I am always, always moving in some small way. Or I’m just rapidly bouncing my foot under the table. And if I catch myself bouncing my foot and force myself to stop, then I just start shifting around in the chair, crossing and uncrossing my legs, leaning one way and then the other. \n\nMy mother-in-law actually asked me at Easter dinner if my dining chair was broken or uncomfortable because I just could not stop adjusting my posture! It was honestly so embarrassing, because in my head, I thought I was doing such a good job of hiding it. I thought I looked perfectly still and polite! But no matter how hard I try to just sit there and look composed, my body is just constantly finding these little ways to keep moving. So yes, the inability to sit still has always been there since I was a little girl, it just got a bit smaller and more contained, I guess.\n\nDoctor: Do you also have trouble paying close attention to details or making careless mistakes in your day-to-day tasks?\n\nPatient: Oh, gosh, yes. It is honestly one of the most frustrating things about how my brain works, because I really do try. I mean, I try so, so hard to be careful. Since I'm not working outside the house right now, I naturally take on a lot of the administrative stuff for our family, and I volunteer quite a bit—PTA, church committees, helping out with the kids' extracurriculars, that sort of thing. So I am constantly dealing with schedules and planning.\n\nAnd I will sit down to put together, say, a volunteer sign-up sheet for a school event, or I’ll be working on our household budget—like those Sunday night sessions I was telling you about—and I will spend all this time on it. I will go over it, I'll look at the screen, and I will genuinely think to myself, 'Okay, this looks great, I've checked it, it's all correct and good to go.' \n\nBut then, almost without fail, I will look at it later, or someone else will point it out to me, and I’ll realize that I made these just completely silly, careless mistakes. Or with the budget, I will have reversed numbers. I'll type 45 instead of 54, and of course, that completely throws the whole month's math off and my husband has to go back in and fix it. \n\nAnd it drives me absolutely crazy because I really, truly thought I had checked it! I swear I looked right at that date or that number, and my brain just somehow told me it was correct. My eyes just glide right over the errors. It’s so embarrassing, especially when it’s something public like an email going out to thirty other parents, because people must think I just don't care enough to proofread my work. But I do! I spend so much time trying to make sure it's right. Like just last month, I was doing the parent volunteer roster for the spring festival, and I spent a good forty-five minutes making sure the formatting was pretty and the fonts matched, but then I managed to send it out with the wrong month at the top. It's just a constant battle with the little details like that, no matter how much effort I put into double-checking myself.\n\n[Instruction]\n- Give candidates as ICD-10 codes, not disease names.\n- If the list changed from the previous candidates, say in \"note\" what this turn added or ruled out. My eyes were moving across the page, I was physically looking at the words, but my brain just completely stopped recording the information. I’ll have to flip back two or three pages just to figure out where I actually checked out. \n\nAnd it’s not just with fun things like reading for a book club. It happens with the important, day-to-day stuff, too. Since I’m not working right now, I handle a lot of the household organizing and the school committee stuff. So, I'll get these long planning emails from, say, the PTA president. She's lovely, but she writes these massive, detailed updates about the spring carnival or the logistics for the teacher appreciation luncheon. I’ll sit down at my laptop to read it, completely determined to get it done, and I start out fine. But halfway down the screen, the exact same thing happens. I’m just staring at a block of text about volunteer shifts or napkin colors, and nothing is registering. \n\nIt takes me forever to get through anything that requires me to just sit and focus, because I have to keep rereading the same sentences four or five times before the meaning actually sticks in my head long enough for me to process it. It’s not that I don’t care about the spring carnival, you know? It’s just like my attention span has this tiny little expiration timer on it, and once those first few minutes are up, the timer goes off and my focus just completely dissolves, even if I'm staring right at the thing I'm supposed to be concentrating on. So, yes, to answer your question, sustaining attention is definitely a major, major issue for me.\n\nDoctor: Before age 12, did you have these same kinds of attention or activity problems in more than one place, like both at home and at school?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. It is funny you ask about that specific age, because honestly, looking back, this was already a huge part of who I was way back in elementary school. I mean, it was incredibly obvious even then. I was always, and I mean always, the girl with the incredibly messy desk. You know how teachers would do those desk organization checks on Friday afternoons? Mine was just a complete disaster zone of crumpled up worksheets and stray crayons and old snack wrappers. \n\nAnd oh my goodness, the forgotten permission slips. My mother used to get so incredibly frustrated with me because I would pull out a permission slip for a field trip or a pizza day that was shoved all the way at the very bottom of my backpack, completely destroyed and unreadable, and it would already be three days past the deadline. She was always having to call the school office to beg them to let me go on the trip anyway.\n\nAnd the parent-teacher conferences were always exactly the same, year after year. My parents were constantly getting notes sent home from my teachers saying that I talked out of turn, or that I seemed completely unable to stay seated during lessons. The teachers would always tell my parents that I was a sweet girl, but I was just constantly interrupting the lesson or wandering around the classroom to sharpen my pencil for the fifth time or go look out the window. \n\nAnd it definitely was not just at school, either. It was the exact same story at home, which used to drive my dad crazy. My parents were always getting onto me for jumping up from the dinner table before we were excused, or I would be sent upstairs to clean my room and my mom would come in an hour later and I would be playing with some old toy I found under the bed, with the room just as messy as when I started. So yes, it was definitely happening in both places. It is like I have just always been this way, even when I was seven or eight years old, just constantly buzzing around and losing track of absolutely everything I was supposed to be doing.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel internally restless or like you need to move around, even when you’re trying to sit still?\n\nPatient: Oh, yes, absolutely. That internal feeling... that's exactly it. It's actually a big part of what finally made me decide to come in and talk to someone, because I just feel like I can't settle in my own body anymore. It's this constant, buzzing sort of tension right under my skin. \n\nIt's the worst when I'm supposed to be sitting quietly and handling things, you know? Like, my husband and I try to sit down on Sunday evenings to go over the shared household plans for the week—the kids' schedules, the meal planning, the budget, all that necessary paperwork that keeps a family running. He's very methodical about it, he'll have his laptop open and his little spreadsheet pulled up, and he just sits there, perfectly content to go through it line by line. \n\nBut me? I sit down next to him, and almost immediately, I feel this... this pressure building up inside my chest and my legs. It's not always that I'm actually getting up and running around the room, though sometimes I do suddenly remember that I need to go check the laundry or grab a glass of water just to have an excuse to stand up. But even when I force myself to stay planted in the chair next to him, internally, I feel like a motor that's just revving and revving with nowhere to go. My mind is screaming at me to move, to stretch, to just *do* something other than sit there looking at the calendar. \n\nI'll try to take deep breaths, or I'll grip the edge of the table, just trying to force that restless feeling down so we can finish figuring out who is picking up our youngest from soccer practice on Thursday. It's like my body is telling me that sitting still is somehow an emergency that I need to escape from. So yes, even when I'm physically staying in one spot, inside, I'm just pacing back and forth, completely unable to just settle down and be at peace.\n\nDoctor: Were you also this fidgety and unable to sit still as a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, completely. I mean, like I was saying before about jumping up from the dinner table when I was seven or eight, it was definitely there back then. I was always in motion. Society kind of expects you to sit down and act like an adult. I’ll have entered the completely wrong date for the bake sale—like, I'll put down a Tuesday when it's obviously supposed to be a Thursday—or I'll have just entirely skipped a line on the spreadsheet so the time slots don't make any sense at all. Oh, definitely. "Always on the go," a "whirlwind," "driven by a motor"—my mom used all of those phrases to describe me when I was little. I just never, ever stopped moving. And honestly? It is exhausting, honestly, because in my head I am trying so hard to project this image of a calm, collected adult woman, but my body is just rebelling the entire time. And it is not just the big movements, it is the little ones too, the ring twisting, the foot tapping. I just do not understand how other people can just sit there like statues. They just sit and listen, and I am practically doing a whole workout in my seat just trying to keep all that nervous energy contained. Social activities or sports? Um... you know, I haven't really noticed it happening in those situations, to be honest. Which is kind of funny when you think about it, given how much I struggle everywhere else. 

But no, like, I play in a casual tennis group—well, it's more like a glorified hitting-around session with some other moms from the neighborhood on Tuesday mornings. We play at the community center, the one over on Elm Street that just got their courts resurfaced? They did a really beautiful job, by the way. It used to be so cracked and dangerous, you'd trip if you weren't careful. But anyway, when I'm playing tennis, or even when I go out for dinner with my girlfriends or go to our monthly book club, I don't really have those same issues at all. 

Like, with the book club—which is honestly just an excuse for us to drink Pinot Grigio and catch up, we barely even talk about the books anymore. Last month we were supposed to read that new historical fiction novel everyone is talking about, the one with the blue cover, and I think maybe two of us actually finished it. But when I'm there, sitting in someone's living room, I'm totally fine. I don't get that awful restless, buzzing feeling, and I'm not, you know, zoning out or forgetting what people are saying to me. Oh, constantly. It is honestly one of the things that frustrates me—and probably my husband, if we're being completely honest—the absolute most. It’s just this endless cycle of... well, I keep meaning to do these totally basic, everyday things, and they just completely vanish from my mind the second I look away. 

Like returning phone calls. I’ll see a missed call or a voicemail from a friend, or my sister, and I’ll tell myself, "Okay, I just need to finish wiping down these counters and then I will sit down and call her right back." But then I get distracted by the sponge needing to be replaced, or the dog barking at the mailman, and before I know it, literally three or four entire days will pass. I keep meaning to return the call, I really do, but it just evaporates from my brain until she texts me asking if I'm ignoring her. 

And it’s the exact same thing with paying bills. We put as much as we can on autopay, thank goodness, because otherwise our electricity would probably get shut off on a regular basis. But for the random ones that come in the mail, like a copay from the pediatrician or the quarterly water bill? I will put the envelope right in the middle of the kitchen island so I can’t possibly ignore it. I keep meaning to pay it, I'll even leave a pen sitting right on top of it, but then it just becomes part of the scenery, you know? I walk past it fifty times and completely forget it exists until a late notice shows up in the mail. 

And don't even get me started on leaving the house. If I have to bring something to a meeting—like the sign-in sheets for that church committee I was telling you about, or even just a tray of muffins I baked for the volunteers—I will tell myself all morning not to forget it. I’ll even put it by the door! But somehow, I’ll grab my purse, walk right past the item, and I’m already in the car, sometimes halfway down my street or even pulling into the church parking lot, before it suddenly hits me that I left the stuff sitting right there on the entryway table. It makes me feel so flaky and unreliable, but I just... I literally cannot hold onto the thought long enough to actually do the thing.

Oh, gosh... yes. Yes, I definitely do that. And it’s honestly so embarrassing for me because I really, truly care a lot about being respectful. I was raised in a household where you do *not* interrupt, you know? It was pretty much the cardinal rule of politeness growing up. If someone pauses for even half a second to find a word, I’m instantly throwing out five different options for what they might be trying to say. It’s not that I think what I have to say is more important, or that I’m trying to be rude—I’m really not! It’s just that... the thought pops into my head, and the response just comes flying out of my mouth before I’ve even made myself wait. 

It’s like there’s absolutely no pause button between my brain and my vocal cords. It's incredibly frustrating because I know how it comes across, but I just can't seem to hold the thought in.

You know, actually... no, not really. That’s one thing that I don't really struggle with, at least not in the sense of physically getting up and walking away. If I’m somewhere where there is a very clear, formal expectation that I need to be in a chair, I will stay in that chair.

My kids are even starting to notice—they'll ask me three times if I remembered to sign a form, and it just kills me that they feel like they have to manage me.\n\nDoctor: When you were a child, did teachers or your parents ever describe you as 'always on the go'?\n\nPatient: Oh, definitely. \"Always on the go,\" a \"whirlwind,\" \"driven by a motor\"—my mom used all of those phrases to describe me when I was little. I just never, ever stopped moving. And honestly? That really hasn't changed at all. It's exactly the same now, it just looks a little different because I'm an adult. So I sit down to do that, but while the inbox is loading, I'll notice the kitchen junk drawer is sticking a little bit, so I just start pulling everything out of it to reorganize it—the rubber bands, the dead batteries, the old takeout menus, just everything piled up on the counter. And then halfway through sorting the rubber bands, I'll suddenly panic about whether I scheduled the kids' dentist appointments, so I completely abandon the drawer to go check the calendar on the wall in the hallway. \n\nI just move from the laundry to the emails to reorganizing a drawer to checking the calendar without really taking a break at all. It's exhausting, honestly. It's not even like I'm consciously choosing to do it, it feels more like... well, like I’m being pushed from the inside? Like there's this internal pressure that just forces me to keep bouncing from one thing to the next to the next. I don't even realize I haven't sat down for four hours until my feet start aching. It's just this constant, restless energy that I absolutely cannot turn off, no matter how much I might want to just sit still for five minutes.\n\nDoctor: Do you often make decisions or act without thinking first?\n\nPatient: Act without thinking? It's actually kind of funny because you would think, given how much I'm physically bouncing off the walls and jumping from the laundry to the emails like I just told you, that I'd just snap-decide things or do things on a whim, but it's actually the complete opposite. \n\nIf anything, I am a terrible overthinker. I take way, way too long to make a decision because I feel like I have to research every single possible angle before I do anything. Like, just last week, our toaster oven broke. The heating element just completely gave out right when I was trying to heat up some snacks for the kids after school. And instead of just running to Target and grabbing a basic replacement like a normal person probably would, I spent... well, I kid you not, probably three whole days reading reviews on different models. \n\nI had at least fifteen tabs open on my laptop at any given time, comparing the wattage, whether it had an air-fryer feature, if the crumb tray was removable from the front or the back—which is actually a really huge deal for cleaning, by the way, because if it pulls out from the back, you have to pull the whole heavy unit away from the wall every time you want to empty it, and our counter space is already so limited with the coffee maker and the stand mixer. Anyway, my husband was just begging me, he was like, \"Please, just buy a toaster, any toaster,\" but I couldn't just pick one without being absolutely certain it was the right choice. I had to read the one-star reviews to see what the worst-case scenarios were. \n\nSo, no, I definitely don't just act without thinking.
